title: A fractional quantum Hall factory on quantum processors: constant-depth preparation of clustered non-Abelian states
authors: Cheng Xu, Ching Hua Lee, Hong-Hao Tu, Yang Zhang
abstract: Non-Abelian anyons arise as exotic excitations in fractional quantum Hall (FQH) matter and have proved very elusive to realize in conventional platforms. In this work, we show that on a programmable quantum hardware platform, the more exotic FQH excitations are the less costly ones to prepare: clustered non-Abelian FQH states admit parallel quantum preparation circuits whose two-qubit depth is independent of system size, while constructing the more common Abelian Laughlin state requires a sequential circuit chain with linear depth. The centerpiece of this work is our new systematic framework for cataloging possible FQH states and preparing them on quantum circuits at unprecedented scale and variety. Our prepared parafermionic Read--Rezayi $\mathbb{Z}_3$ state holds depth 3 from 8 to 118 qubits, and full root sampling extends to a 154-qubit, 104-electron Read--Rezayi $\mathbb{Z}_4$ state. In all, our demonstrated 18-family catalog of prepared FQH states extends to all 156 qubits of an IBM Heron processor, limited only by existing hardware scale. Measurements on the prepared states recover the expected fractional quasihole charges, with the charge estimator exact in every symmetry-selected shot for the clustered states, and braiding data of the non-Abelian $e/4$ quasihole measured via interferometric extensions. Our work establishes a scalable route to studying FQH physics on quantum processors and opens new avenues for preparing and probing non-Abelian topological matter far beyond the reach of conventional platforms.
summary: The paper presents a scalable method to simulate exotic Fractional Quantum Hall states on quantum processors. It demonstrates that non-Abelian clustered FQH states can be prepared with constant circuit depth, contrasting sharply with the linear depth required for simpler Abelian states. This establishes a powerful new route for studying topological matter beyond current hardware limitations.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a scalable method to prepare exotic Fractional Quantum Hall (FQH) states, particularly those exhibiting non-Abelian anyon statistics, on programmable quantum hardware.
main_result: Clustered non-Abelian FQH states can be prepared using parallel quantum circuits with a two-qubit depth independent of system size (constant depth), unlike the Abelian Laughlin state which requires linearly growing circuit depth.
method: The authors use a systematic framework to catalog FQH states by constructing parent Hamiltonians from pattern-of-zeros data, translating these into quantum circuits for implementation on hardware like IBM Heron processors.
model_or_system: The study focuses on FQH matter, modeling various states including the Abelian Laughlin state and non-Abelian Read–Rezayi $\mathbb{Z}_3$ and $\mathbb{Z}_4$ states. These are analyzed using thin-torus circuits derived from pseudopotential parent Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Fractional quasihole charges, non-Abelian braiding data (measured interferometrically), and circuit depth scaling.
important_parameters: System size (up to 156 qubits), two-qubit gate depth, and the clustering property of the state wavefunction.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation at large scales is identified as per-qubit readout error rather than the gate count itself; constant depth relies on junction squeezes forming disjoint blocks.
figures_summary: Figures compare circuit depth scaling, illustrating the dichotomy between linear depth (Laughlin) and constant depth (clustered non-Abelian states) for various FQH models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing a systematic framework to cataloging states, demonstrating the circuit construction pipeline, comparing depth scalings based on clustering properties, and finally validating results by measuring topological observables like fractional charge and braiding data.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete quantum circuit blueprints for simulating highly complex, strongly correlated electron phenomena (FQH physics) that are otherwise inaccessible due to exponential resource scaling in traditional methods.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The clustering dichotomy (linear vs. constant circuit depth) for state preparation across our FQH catalog. (a) Routed two-qubit depth after transpilation against qubit count for six families of FQH states we prepared: the two chained Laughlin recursions, the fermionic ν = 1/3 and the dual-rail bosonic ν = 1/2, both grow linearly, while the clustered Moore–Read (to 98 qubits), Read–Rezayi Z3 (to 118), and Gaffnian (to 97) hold constant depth three, and the Haffnian, whose squeeze runs two levels deep, sits at depth 8 to 16. Open dashed markers are the depth-16 ibm kingston registers that extend the Haffnian clean ladder to 104 qubits. Beyond roughly 120 qubits, heavy-hex routing...

FIG. 2. How the 2-qubit gate depth scales depends cru- cially on the clustering properties of the FQH state to be prepared. (a) Laughlin ν = 1/3 (root 100 100 100): consecu- tive junction squeezes share an electron, so the flag rotations form a sequential chain and the depth grows with size. (b) Read–Rezayi Z3 (root 11100 11100): junctions couple disjoint electron pairs and fire in parallel at constant depth. The junc- tion squeezes Ji and their amplitudes are defined in Sec. II C [Eq. (2)], the flag-rotation circuits in the same subsection, and the four-family gallery with circuit sketches in Fig. S2 of the Appendix [55].

FIG. 3. Workflow of our FQH state construction and mea- surement (N: particle number; K: total momentum around the cylinder; the kernel count is the zero-mode degeneracy of Eq. (1)). Each family’s pattern-of-zeros data enters at the top box. We construct its parent Hamiltonian from that data and certify it back against the same data (kernel count against the (k, r)-admissibility count, thin-torus limit against the root pattern), and only the certified zero-mode kernel then supplies the circuit amplitudes, the acceptance certificates, the posts- election quantum numbers, and the response protocols.

FIG. 4. Transpiled two-qubit cost against qubit count across the catalog. Filled markers are the exact-verification window, where every circuit carries an exact-diagonalization fidelity (Table I); open markers continue each family along its flown scaling ladder to chip scale, up to 154 qubits, at the routed depths listed in the footnotes of Table S5 of the Appendix [55]. Hue encodes the structural branch: chained Abelian (blues, shown over the verification window; their chip-scale depth scaling is in Fig. 1), clustered non-Abelian and non-unitary (greens and oranges), and multi-rail multicomponent (violets). The gray band is the variational route to the isotropic point (Sec. V).
